oop-1.title: The Big Picture
oop-1.lead: Object-oriented programming turns a problem into cooperating objects with clear responsibilities.
oop-1.objective: Explain how OOP differs from procedural decomposition and identify the four core principles.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Procedural programs organize behavior into functions. OOP additionally packages state and behavior into objects, making it easier to model a domain and protect its rules as a program grows.

concepts.title: Abstraction
concepts.text: Expose the important idea while hiding distracting detail.

concepts.title: Encapsulation
concepts.text: Keep state and the operations that protect it together.

concepts.title: Polymorphism
concepts.text: Use one interface for multiple compatible implementations.

oop-1.note: When designing a class, name the responsibility it owns before choosing its fields.

oop.title: The Big Picture
oop.lead: Object-oriented programming turns a problem into cooperating objects with clear responsibilities.
oop.objective: Explain how OOP differs from procedural decomposition and identify the four core principles.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Procedural programs organize behavior into functions. OOP additionally packages state and behavior into objects, making it easier to model a domain and protect its rules as a program grows.

concepts.title: Abstraction
concepts.text: Expose the important idea while hiding distracting detail.

concepts.title: Encapsulation
concepts.text: Keep state and the operations that protect it together.

concepts.title: Polymorphism
concepts.text: Use one interface for multiple compatible implementations.

oop.note: When designing a class, name the responsibility it owns before choosing its fields.

oop-2.title: Structure & Classes
oop-2.lead: Structures and classes give related data a shape that the rest of a program can understand.
oop-2.objective: Create a simple class, distinguish a class from an object, and choose an appropriate member visibility.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A class is a blueprint; an object is a concrete instance of that blueprint. C++ structures default to public access, while classes default to private access, but both can contain fields, methods, and constructors.

concepts.title: Blueprint
concepts.text: A class defines the possible state and behavior.

concepts.title: Instance
concepts.text: An object occupies memory and has its own state.

concepts.title: Visibility
concepts.text: Access control communicates which operations are safe to call.

oop-2.note: Keep public methods small and make invalid state difficult to represent.

oop-3.title: Objects & Classes
oop-3.lead: Good objects protect their own rules. Constructors create valid objects and encapsulation keeps their internal state intentional.
oop-3.objective: Explain constructors, destructors, overloading, and the role of encapsulation in a class design.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A constructor is the first conversation between a class and the object it creates. It gives the object a known starting point instead of leaving its state to chance. A destructor releases owned resources when the object leaves its lifetime.

concepts.title: A boundary
concepts.text: Private state creates a boundary around the rules an object must protect.

concepts.title: A promise
concepts.text: A constructor promises that a new object begins in a usable state.

concepts.title: A reason to change
concepts.text: Clear responsibilities make future changes smaller and safer.

oop-3.note: Prefer member initializer lists in C++ and make ownership explicit.

oop-4.title: Constructors & Class State
oop-4.lead: Class state has a lifetime, and constructors let you make that lifetime predictable.
oop-4.objective: Use default, parameterized, const, and static members safely.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A default constructor supplies sensible defaults. Static members belong to the class rather than one object, while const members cannot change after initialization and therefore must be initialized in the constructor.

concepts.title: Defaults
concepts.text: Useful defaults reduce invalid partially initialized objects.

concepts.title: Lifetime
concepts.text: Static storage lasts independently of any single instance.

concepts.title: Const correctness
concepts.text: Const communicates and enforces an operation that does not mutate state.

oop-4.note: Document whether a class owns a value, borrows it, or shares it.

oop-5.title: Functions & Overloading
oop-5.lead: Functions become easier to use when their interfaces express intent without unnecessary repetition.
oop-5.objective: Apply overloading, inline functions, default arguments, and storage-class ideas.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Overloaded functions share a name but differ in parameter lists. Default arguments make common calls concise, while inline is a request to the compiler and not a guarantee about generated machine code.

concepts.title: Signature
concepts.text: Parameters determine which overload is selected.

concepts.title: Defaults
concepts.text: Use defaults for stable optional behavior, not ambiguous APIs.

concepts.title: Scope
concepts.text: Storage and visibility determine where a name can be used.

oop-5.note: Avoid overload sets that make a call difficult for a reader to resolve.

oop-6.title: Composition & Aggregation
oop-6.lead: Composition models objects that are built from other objects, while aggregation models a looser relationship.
oop-6.objective: Choose between composition and aggregation when modeling a real system.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A Car has an Engine as a compositional part when the engine lifetime belongs to the car. A university aggregates Student objects because students exist independently. The relationship should reflect ownership and lifetime, not just vocabulary.

concepts.title: Has-a
concepts.text: Composition describes a strong owned part relationship.

concepts.title: Uses-a
concepts.text: Aggregation or association can refer to an independent object.

concepts.title: Lifetime
concepts.text: Ownership decides who creates and destroys a resource.

oop-6.note: Draw ownership arrows before writing constructors or destructors.

oop-7.title: Inheritance
oop-7.lead: Inheritance expresses an is-a relationship and lets a derived class specialize a base interface.
oop-7.objective: Build a hierarchy with correct access control and explain abstract classes.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A derived class reuses a base class interface, but inheritance should represent substitutability rather than code sharing alone. Protected members are available to derived classes; private members remain behind the base interface.

concepts.title: Substitutability
concepts.text: A derived object should work wherever its base is expected.

concepts.title: Access
concepts.text: Public, protected, and private inheritance change the exposed interface.

concepts.title: Abstractness
concepts.text: Pure virtual functions describe behavior without an implementation.

oop-7.note: Favor composition when the relationship is not genuinely is-a.

oop-8.title: Multiple Inheritance
oop-8.lead: Multiple inheritance combines more than one base interface, but it also creates ambiguity that must be designed away.
oop-8.objective: Resolve ambiguity and compare multiple inheritance with composition.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: If two bases provide a member with the same name, a derived class must qualify the call or override the behavior. Virtual base classes solve the diamond problem by sharing one common base subobject.

concepts.title: Ambiguity
concepts.text: Qualified names make the intended base explicit.

concepts.title: Diamond
concepts.text: Repeated base state can be shared through virtual inheritance.

concepts.title: Design cost
concepts.text: Composition often gives the same reuse with simpler ownership.

oop-8.note: Use multiple inheritance primarily for orthogonal interfaces, not a tangled implementation hierarchy.

oop-9.title: Operator Overloading
oop-9.lead: Operator overloading can make value-like types readable when the meaning of an operator stays intuitive.
oop-9.objective: Overload unary and binary operators and avoid surprising conversions.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: An overloaded operator is still a function with a clear contract. A Vector can define addition because vector addition has a natural meaning; a domain type should not overload an operator merely to save a few characters.

concepts.title: Symmetry
concepts.text: Binary operators should usually treat both operands consistently.

concepts.title: Value semantics
concepts.text: Return new values when the operation does not mutate either operand.

concepts.title: Conversions
concepts.text: Explicit conversions prevent accidental and lossy behavior.

oop-9.note: Keep overloaded operators unsurprising for someone who already knows the language.

oop-10.title: Pointers
oop-10.lead: Pointers expose addresses and make dynamic data structures possible, but they require disciplined ownership.
oop-10.objective: Use pointer operators, dynamic allocation, and safe cleanup.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: The address-of operator obtains an address and dereferencing reads or writes the pointed-to object. Memory allocated with new must be released with delete, and a pointer should never outlive the object it refers to.

concepts.title: Indirection
concepts.text: A pointer stores where a value lives, not the value itself.

concepts.title: Ownership
concepts.text: The owner is responsible for releasing dynamic memory.

concepts.title: Safety
concepts.text: Null and dangling pointers are invalid states to prevent.

oop-10.note: Prefer RAII and smart pointers in modern C++ when a raw pointer is not required.

oop-11.title: Virtual Functions
oop-11.lead: Virtual functions defer method selection until runtime so a base reference can call derived behavior.
oop-11.objective: Explain late binding, virtual destructors, and abstract interfaces.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: With a virtual function, the runtime chooses the override based on the actual object type. A polymorphic base should usually have a virtual destructor so deleting through a base pointer destroys the complete derived object.

concepts.title: Late binding
concepts.text: The runtime type determines the override that runs.

concepts.title: Interface
concepts.text: An abstract base defines a contract for derived classes.

concepts.title: Cleanup
concepts.text: Virtual destruction preserves the derived cleanup path.

oop-11.note: Use override on derived methods so the compiler checks the intended relationship.

oop-12.title: Polymorphism & Friends
oop-12.lead: Friends and static members are specialized tools for collaboration between objects and the class itself.
oop-12.objective: Use friend functions, friend classes, and static methods with deliberate boundaries.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A friend can access private members without becoming a member, which is useful for symmetric operators or tightly coupled helpers. Static functions have no this pointer and can operate only on static state or explicit arguments.

concepts.title: Narrow privilege
concepts.text: Grant friendship to the smallest helper that needs it.

concepts.title: Class state
concepts.text: Static data represents shared state and needs one definition.

concepts.title: Polymorphism
concepts.text: Dynamic dispatch lets clients depend on behavior rather than concrete classes.

oop-12.note: Friendship is not inherited or transitive, so treat it as a precise design choice.

oop-13.title: Streams & Files
oop-13.lead: Streams provide a uniform interface for console, string, and file input and output.
oop-13.objective: Read and write files and explain stream state and file pointers.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: An fstream combines input and output, while ifstream and ofstream communicate intent. A failed extraction sets a stream state flag, so loops should test the stream rather than assume every read succeeded.

concepts.title: Abstraction
concepts.text: The stream interface hides device-specific details.

concepts.title: State flags
concepts.text: eof, fail, and bad distinguish common I/O failures.

concepts.title: Position
concepts.text: Seek and tell operations control the file pointer.

oop-13.note: Always check that a file opened successfully before reading or writing.

oop-14.title: Error Handling & File I/O
oop-14.lead: Robust file programs treat I/O as fallible and keep persistence code separate from domain logic.
oop-14.objective: Handle file errors and organize file operations as class responsibilities.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Opening, reading, parsing, and writing can each fail. Report the failure with useful context and leave the object in a predictable state instead of silently accepting partial data.

concepts.title: Validation
concepts.text: Check paths, formats, and stream state at the boundary.

concepts.title: Recovery
concepts.text: A caller should know whether an operation succeeded.

concepts.title: Separation
concepts.text: Persistence methods should not leak file details into every client.

oop-14.note: Test missing files, malformed records, and interrupted writes explicitly.

oop-15.title: Multiple Programs
oop-15.lead: Larger programs need boundaries between declarations, implementations, and build artifacts.
oop-15.objective: Organize headers, source files, directories, and project units.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Header files declare interfaces and source files define behavior. Include guards or pragma once prevent duplicate declarations, while a project build links separate translation units into one executable.

concepts.title: Interface
concepts.text: A header communicates what clients may use.

concepts.title: Implementation
concepts.text: A source file hides how the interface works.

concepts.title: Build
concepts.text: Compilation and linking are distinct stages.

oop-15.note: Keep a header focused and include only the dependencies it truly needs.

oop-16.title: Templates & Exceptions
oop-16.lead: Templates express algorithms and containers once, while exceptions make failure paths explicit.
oop-16.objective: Write function and class templates and handle exceptions without hiding failures.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A template is instantiated for a concrete type when used. Exceptions transfer control to a handler, so code should throw meaningful errors, catch at an appropriate boundary, and clean up through RAII.

concepts.title: Genericity
concepts.text: Templates let one algorithm work across compatible types.

concepts.title: Contract
concepts.text: Exceptions communicate that a normal result could not be produced.

concepts.title: Cleanup
concepts.text: Stack unwinding should leave owned resources safely released.

oop-16.note: Catch by const reference and avoid using exceptions for ordinary branching.

dsa-1.title: Foundations & Arrays
dsa-1.lead: Arrays make indexed data compact and fast to access, which makes them a foundation for many structures.
dsa-1.objective: Choose arrays for suitable workloads and analyze their basic operations.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: An array stores elements contiguously. Index access is O(1), but inserting in the middle shifts later values and costs O(n). Fixed arrays have stable storage; dynamic arrays resize when capacity is exhausted.

concepts.title: Indexing
concepts.text: Address arithmetic makes direct access constant time.

concepts.title: Shifting
concepts.text: Middle insertion and deletion move a suffix of elements.

concepts.title: Capacity
concepts.text: Dynamic arrays trade occasional resizing for flexible length.

dsa-1.note: Start an analysis with the operation the workload performs most often.

dsa.title: Foundations & Arrays
dsa.lead: Arrays make indexed data compact and fast to access, which makes them a foundation for many structures.
dsa.objective: Choose arrays for suitable workloads and analyze their basic operations.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: An array stores elements contiguously. Index access is O(1), but inserting in the middle shifts later values and costs O(n). Fixed arrays have stable storage; dynamic arrays resize when capacity is exhausted.

concepts.title: Indexing
concepts.text: Address arithmetic makes direct access constant time.

concepts.title: Shifting
concepts.text: Middle insertion and deletion move a suffix of elements.

concepts.title: Capacity
concepts.text: Dynamic arrays trade occasional resizing for flexible length.

dsa.note: Start an analysis with the operation the workload performs most often.

dsa-2.title: Linked Lists
dsa-2.lead: Linked lists trade direct indexing for flexible node connections.
dsa-2.objective: Traverse and modify singly and circular linked lists.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A node stores data and a pointer to the next node. Inserting after a known node is O(1), while finding that node is O(n). A circular list connects its tail back to its head and needs careful stopping conditions.

concepts.title: Node
concepts.text: Data and linkage form one independently allocated unit.

concepts.title: Traversal
concepts.text: Follow links until null or the starting node is reached.

concepts.title: Trade-off
concepts.text: Fast local edits come at the cost of cache locality and indexing.

dsa-2.note: Update links before losing the only pointer to the rest of a list.

dsa-3.title: Doubly Linked Lists
dsa-3.lead: A doubly linked list gives every node two pointers, one forward and one back.
dsa-3.objective: Implement a doubly linked list and explain when it is preferable to a singly linked list.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: The previous pointer enables backward traversal and deletion at a known tail node without scanning from the head. The extra pointer costs memory and every mutation must preserve links in both directions.

concepts.title: Bidirectional
concepts.text: Walk the list in either direction without starting over.

concepts.title: Trade-off
concepts.text: Extra memory buys simpler tail operations.

concepts.title: Symmetry
concepts.text: Head and tail updates follow mirror-image logic.

dsa-3.note: After every mutation, verify head.prev and tail.next are null.

dsa-4.title: Stacks & Queues
dsa-4.lead: Stacks and queues constrain access order so algorithms can model real workflows.
dsa-4.objective: Implement push, pop, enqueue, dequeue, and recognize their applications.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A stack is last-in-first-out and supports top access. A queue is first-in-first-out and supports front removal and rear insertion. Array implementations need either shifting or a moving circular index.

concepts.title: LIFO
concepts.text: Stacks model undo, parsing, and call frames.

concepts.title: FIFO
concepts.text: Queues model scheduling and breadth-first processing.

concepts.title: Amortization
concepts.text: Circular indexing avoids repeated full-array shifts.

dsa-4.note: Define empty and full behavior before implementing an operation.

dsa-5.title: Queues & Deques
dsa-5.lead: Queues, deques, and circular queues give a program controlled access at one or both ends.
dsa-5.objective: Compare queue variants and implement their boundary conditions.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends. A circular queue reuses freed slots by wrapping indices, usually tracking size or distinguishing full from empty with one reserved slot.

concepts.title: Deque
concepts.text: Both ends are active operation points.

concepts.title: Wraparound
concepts.text: Modulo arithmetic reuses a fixed buffer.

concepts.title: Invariant
concepts.text: Front, rear, and size must agree after every operation.

dsa-5.note: Write down the empty, one-item, and full cases as tests.

dsa-6.title: Recursion
dsa-6.lead: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to smaller instances of the same problem.
dsa-6.objective: Identify base and recursive cases and estimate recursion cost.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Every recursive function needs a base case that stops progress and a recursive case that moves toward it. The call stack stores pending work, so deep recursion can consume O(n) space or overflow.

concepts.title: Base case
concepts.text: The smallest solved input ends the recursion.

concepts.title: Reduction
concepts.text: Each call should move closer to the base case.

concepts.title: Stack
concepts.text: Pending calls preserve the context needed on return.

dsa-6.note: Trace two or three calls by hand before optimizing a recursive algorithm.

dsa-7.title: Trees & Binary Trees
dsa-7.lead: Trees represent hierarchical data and support traversals that reveal different views of the same structure.
dsa-7.objective: Represent binary trees and perform depth-first and breadth-first traversals.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A binary tree gives each node at most two children. Preorder visits root-left-right, inorder left-root-right, and postorder left-right-root; level order uses a queue to visit by depth.

concepts.title: Hierarchy
concepts.text: Parent-child links encode nested relationships.

concepts.title: Traversal
concepts.text: The visit order answers different application questions.

concepts.title: Height
concepts.text: The longest root-to-leaf path influences recursive cost.

dsa-7.note: Use a small tree and write the output of each traversal before coding it.

dsa-8.title: BSTs & AVL Trees
dsa-8.lead: Search trees keep ordering information, while AVL trees actively maintain balance.
dsa-8.objective: Insert and search in BSTs and explain AVL rotations.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: In a BST, smaller values go left and larger values go right. Its average search is O(log n), but sorted insertion can make it a chain. AVL rotations restore a bounded balance factor after updates.

concepts.title: Ordering
concepts.text: The invariant makes guided search possible.

concepts.title: Worst case
concepts.text: An unbalanced BST can degrade to O(n).

concepts.title: Rotation
concepts.text: Local pointer changes restore height without losing order.

dsa-8.note: Check the ordering invariant after each rotation, not just the height.

dsa-9.title: Graphs
dsa-9.lead: Graphs model relationships that are not limited to a hierarchy.
dsa-9.objective: Represent graphs and traverse them with BFS and DFS.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: An adjacency matrix gives O(1) edge lookup but uses O(V^2) space. An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space and is efficient for sparse graphs. BFS uses a queue; DFS uses recursion or an explicit stack.

concepts.title: Vertices
concepts.text: Entities become nodes in the relationship model.

concepts.title: Edges
concepts.text: Connections may be directed, undirected, weighted, or unweighted.

concepts.title: Visited set
concepts.text: Marking nodes prevents cycles from causing repeated work.

dsa-9.note: Choose representation from graph density and the query you need to answer.

dsa-10.title: Heaps
dsa-10.lead: Heaps keep the highest-priority element at the root while using a compact array representation.
dsa-10.objective: Maintain a heap and explain heap sort and priority queues.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: In a max heap each parent is at least as large as its children. Parent and child indices map directly in an array, and sift-up or sift-down restores the invariant in O(log n).

concepts.title: Priority
concepts.text: The root gives immediate access to the next item.

concepts.title: Invariant
concepts.text: Every parent-child pair obeys the heap ordering.

concepts.title: Heapify
concepts.text: Bottom-up construction runs in O(n), not O(n log n).

dsa-10.note: Do not confuse a heap with a fully sorted array; only the root is globally extreme.

dsa-11.title: Hashing
dsa-11.lead: Hashing turns a key into an array position for near-constant average lookup.
dsa-11.objective: Explain hash functions, collisions, and load factor.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A hash function maps keys to buckets. Collisions are unavoidable, so chaining stores a bucket collection while open addressing probes for another slot. As load factor rises, performance falls and resizing becomes useful.

concepts.title: Uniformity
concepts.text: A good hash spreads keys across buckets.

concepts.title: Collision
concepts.text: Different keys can map to the same position.

concepts.title: Load factor
concepts.text: Occupancy predicts when a table should resize.

dsa-11.note: A hash table is fast on average, not a guarantee of O(1) in every case.

dsa-12.title: Algorithms & Complexity
dsa-12.lead: Algorithm analysis lets you predict how a solution behaves as its input grows.
dsa-12.objective: Use Big O, Omega, and Theta to compare time and space costs.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Big O describes an upper growth bound, Omega a lower bound, and Theta a tight bound. Ignore constants for growth comparisons, but keep input assumptions and dominant terms explicit.

concepts.title: Growth
concepts.text: Complexity describes scaling, not a stopwatch result.

concepts.title: Dominant term
concepts.text: The fastest-growing term controls large inputs.

concepts.title: Space
concepts.text: Auxiliary memory can matter as much as running time.

dsa-12.note: State what n represents before writing a complexity claim.

dsa-13.title: Sorting I
dsa-13.lead: Simple comparison sorts are valuable because their invariants are easy to see and verify.
dsa-13.objective: Compare selection, insertion, and bubble sort on time, space, and adaptiveness.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Selection sort repeatedly chooses the smallest remaining value. Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix and performs well on nearly sorted input. Bubble sort swaps adjacent inversions and can stop early when a pass makes no swaps.

concepts.title: Invariant
concepts.text: A sorted prefix or suffix makes progress visible.

concepts.title: Adaptiveness
concepts.text: Some algorithms benefit from nearly sorted data.

concepts.title: Stability
concepts.text: Equal elements can retain their original order.

dsa-13.note: Use the same input examples to compare each algorithm fairly.

dsa-14.title: Sorting II
dsa-14.lead: Sorting choices should follow the data shape and the guarantees an application needs.
dsa-14.objective: Practice sorting traces and select an algorithm from its behavior.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Selection, insertion, and bubble sort all take O(n^2) worst-case time, but their constants, stability, and best-case behavior differ. A trace exposes where comparisons and moves are spent.

concepts.title: Comparisons
concepts.text: Count comparisons separately from assignments.

concepts.title: Moves
concepts.text: Insertion shifts values; selection minimizes swaps.

concepts.title: Stability
concepts.text: Stable order can preserve meaning attached to equal keys.

dsa-14.note: Measure a small trace, then confirm the asymptotic result.

dsa-15.title: Divide & Conquer
dsa-15.lead: Divide and conquer breaks a large problem into smaller independent problems and combines their results.
dsa-15.objective: Explain merge sort and quick sort partitioning and compare their costs.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Merge sort divides until subarrays have one item, then merges in order for O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. Quick sort partitions around a pivot and is fast on average, but poor pivots can produce O(n^2) time.

concepts.title: Divide
concepts.text: Smaller subproblems make each local decision manageable.

concepts.title: Combine
concepts.text: The merge or partition step restores global structure.

concepts.title: Pivot
concepts.text: Quick sort performance depends on pivot choices.

dsa-15.note: Write the recurrence or partition sizes before asserting complexity.

dsa-16.title: Greedy Algorithms
dsa-16.lead: Greedy algorithms make the best local choice and rely on proof that local choices lead to a global optimum.
dsa-16.objective: Recognize greedy structure and distinguish it from dynamic programming.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A greedy solution needs a greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Activity selection and minimum spanning tree algorithms work because a local safe choice can be proven. Greedy is not automatically correct for every optimization problem.

concepts.title: Local choice
concepts.text: Choose the best immediate option under a stated rule.

concepts.title: Proof
concepts.text: Exchange arguments or cut properties justify correctness.

concepts.title: Counterexample
concepts.text: A single valid counterexample can disprove a greedy rule.

dsa-16.note: Test a greedy idea against a small adversarial input before implementing it.

dbms-1.title: Database Foundations
dbms-1.lead: A database gives persistent information structure, durability, and controlled access beyond a program run.
dbms-1.objective: Distinguish data, databases, DBMS software, and common database models.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A DBMS stores and retrieves data while providing constraints, transactions, security, and concurrent access. Relational systems organize data into tables, while document and graph models emphasize different relationships.

concepts.title: Persistence
concepts.text: Data survives beyond the process that created it.

concepts.title: Schema
concepts.text: A schema describes permitted structure and relationships.

concepts.title: DBMS
concepts.text: The system enforces storage, query, and integrity behavior.

dbms-1.note: Ask which guarantees the application needs before choosing a database model.

dbms.lead: A database gives persistent information structure, durability, and controlled access beyond a program run.
dbms.objective: Distinguish data, databases, DBMS software, and common database models.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A DBMS stores and retrieves data while providing constraints, transactions, security, and concurrent access. Relational systems organize data into tables, while document and graph models emphasize different relationships.

concepts.title: Persistence
concepts.text: Data survives beyond the process that created it.

concepts.title: Schema
concepts.text: A schema describes permitted structure and relationships.

concepts.title: DBMS
concepts.text: The system enforces storage, query, and integrity behavior.

dbms.note: Ask which guarantees the application needs before choosing a database model.

dbms-2.title: Relational Models
dbms-2.lead: Tables, keys, and relationships form the backbone of every relational database.
dbms-2.objective: Identify primary keys, foreign keys, and relationship types.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: A relational model organizes data into tables where each row is a tuple and each column an attribute. Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys link rows across tables and enforce referential integrity.

concepts.title: Identity
concepts.text: A primary key gives every row a unique handle.

concepts.title: Connection
concepts.text: A foreign key encodes a relationship to another table.

concepts.title: Integrity
concepts.text: Constraints prevent orphaned or ambiguous references.

dbms-2.note: Draw the entity-relationship diagram for a schema before writing queries.

dbms-3.title: SQL Essentials
dbms-3.lead: SQL turns a question about data into a precise, composable query.
dbms-3.objective: Write SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, and JOIN queries.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: SELECT chooses columns, WHERE filters rows before grouping, and ORDER BY controls presentation. JOIN combines related rows; GROUP BY forms groups for aggregate functions such as COUNT and AVG.

concepts.title: Selection
concepts.text: Filter early when it reduces work and clarifies intent.

concepts.title: Join
concepts.text: Match rows through a relationship instead of duplicating data.

concepts.title: Aggregation
concepts.text: Summarize groups with a defined measure.

dbms-3.note: Build a query one clause at a time and inspect its intermediate result.

dbms-4.title: Normalization
dbms-4.lead: Normalization reduces duplication so updates remain consistent and predictable.
dbms-4.objective: Explain 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF and identify update anomalies.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: First normal form keeps values atomic. Second normal form removes partial dependency on part of a composite key. Third normal form removes transitive dependency on a non-key attribute. Normalization separates facts into tables linked by keys.

concepts.title: Redundancy
concepts.text: Repeated facts create more places for inconsistent updates.

concepts.title: Dependency
concepts.text: A functional dependency says which attributes determine others.

concepts.title: Decomposition
concepts.text: Split tables while preserving useful relationships and information.

dbms-4.note: Normalize to protect correctness, then denormalize only for a measured reason.

dbms-5.title: Transactions & Security
dbms-5.lead: Transactions and security protect data when many users and failures meet the same system.
dbms-5.objective: Explain ACID, isolation, commits, rollbacks, and basic database security.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.body: Atomicity makes a transaction all-or-nothing, consistency preserves constraints, isolation controls concurrent visibility, and durability preserves committed data. Parameterized queries and least-privilege roles reduce security risk.

concepts.title: ACID
concepts.text: Four guarantees describe reliable transaction behavior.

concepts.title: Isolation
concepts.text: Concurrent work should not expose unsafe intermediate state.

concepts.title: Least privilege
concepts.text: Users and services should receive only required access.

dbms-5.note: Pair every multi-step write with a clear commit or rollback strategy.
